newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Greens join fight over gene-modified foods.
newsitem.headline: German Greens join fight over gene-modified foods.

text.p: German Green party members on Tuesday sided with consumer and environmentalist lobbies in a bid to block food products using genetically-altered soybeans, or at least to seek labelling of all products using such soya.

"We fear for the safety of consumers and we don't fully know the effect of genetically-modified crops on farming and the environment," Dorothee Freundenberg-Huebner, a member of the Hamburg state parliament said at a news conference.
"We will ask the Hamburg senate (parliament) and the Bonn government to use their influence at EU level to tighten import licensing laws and to provide comprehensive labelling."
The news conference was held ahead of a meeting on Wednesday of the Parliament-Council of Ministers conciliation committee on the draft directive on "novel foods", COM(93)631.
The Greens parliamentary group in Bonn confirmed that the moves at EU level announced in Hamburg were fully in line with its national initiative to revise German food labelling laws.
This was aimed at ensuring consumers were told whether or not a product contained traces of genetically modified ingredients.
The conciliation committee will discuss European Parliament demands to sharpen European Commission proposals on health and safety standards for genetically engineered foods.
"The Bonn government supported EU clearance of imports of genetically-modified U.S. soybeans for processing earlier this year," said Green MEP Hiltrud Breyer, a committee member.

"We want legislators to rethink their position by making clear there are no checks in place to exclude the illegal marketing and seeds use of such imported beans -- as opposed to their stipulated crushing," she said.
"We also believe not telling consumers what they are eating is an offense against their civil rights."
"There are fears some genetic modifications could be dangerous for people with allergies and strengthen their immunity to antibiotics."

Breyer said labelling should ensure that not only major changes to a foodstuff would appear on the final product's label, but the use of raw materials derived from genetically-altered organisms should also be indicated.
If it could be excluded that those organisms had been used, then the industry should have no problem saying so.
Breyer said polls conducted on behalf of environmentalist group Greenpeace showed some 80 percent of consumers opposed gene-altered foods and 90 percent wanted labelling.
The left-wing Greens said they supported moves by Greenpeace and consumer organisations to ostracise gene-altered U.S. soybean imports, due in a few weeks' time.
Developed by Monsanto Co, the beans are resistant to a weed-killer and to date account for just one or two percent of the total U.S. crop.
But farmers, wishing to avoid extra costs, have no plans to segregate.
Germany, the EU's leading oilseeds consumers, processed some 3.4 million tonnes of soybeans in 1995 out of a total seeds crush of seven million.
An estimated 60 percent came from the U.S.
Soy oil is used in about 30 percent of all food products.
Since the start of the Greenpeace campaign, unmodified domestic rape oil has reached and maintained an unusual premium over soy oil in Rotterdam vegetable oil markets.
